In remove(), storedIdp is fetched from idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) before removal, which is correct, but registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp) is called with storedIdp possibly null if the alias doesn't exist. getLoginPredicate().test(idp) does handle null via Objects::nonNull check, so this is safe, but note that in the invalid branch (isInvalid(cacheKey)), registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) is also called with potentially null storedIdp passed into registerIDPInvalidation which calls idp.getInternalId() without a null check, causing a NullPointerException if the alias does not match any identity provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider misuses KeyStore provider as 'the' BC provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider backing KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(). This is fragile: the default keystore type's provider is not necessarily BouncyCastle (it could be SUN, PKCS11, etc. depending on JVM/platform configuration), yet CryptoProvider callers elsewhere in the codebase assume this method returns a BC-compatible provider. This can silently return the wrong provider on some platforms, causing unexpected failures or incorrect security provider usage downstream.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead/wasted ASN1Encoder calls before building actual sequence

In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, two throwaway ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls are made (lines 114-115) whose results are discarded entirely before building the real DER sequence a few lines later. This is dead code that does nothing useful, wastes allocations, and is confusing/misleading to maintainers reading the encoding logic — it looks like a leftover from development that should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for third-party CryptoProvider implementations

Adding a new non-default abstract method order() to the CryptoProvider interface is a breaking change for any third-party or external implementations of this interface (e.g. keycloak-client repo or other consumers) that are not updated to implement it. Since this is a public SPI interface loaded via ServiceLoader, this will cause compile and runtime failures for existing implementations until they add the method. Consider providing a default implementation to preserve backward compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Silent provider selection replaces previous fail-fast behavior on multiple providers

Previously, detecting multiple CryptoProvider implementations on the classpath threw IllegalStateException to force explicit configuration. Now it silently picks the provider with the highest order() and only logs at debug level which providers were ignored. In production deployments where debug logging is disabled, this means a misconfigured classpath with multiple incompatible crypto providers (e.g., accidentally bundling authz-client with the main server) will silently select one without any visible warning, which can hide subtle and hard-to-diagnose cryptographic configuration errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mismatched resource lookup key in hasPermission(ClientModel, String) vs. resource creation

`hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope)` looks up `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())`, using the client's internal id as resource name. But resources for individual clients are created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` using `name = resolveClient(session, id)` which resolves to `client.getId()` as well, so this should match — however the owner parameter passed is `server.getId()` whereas resources are created with owner `resourceServer.getClientId()` (see `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())`). If `server.getId()` differs from `resourceServer.getClientId()` (likely, since one is the resource-server's internal id, the other is the owning client's id), this lookup will never find existing per-client resources, breaking the per-client manage/view/configure checks and effectively relying only on the all-clients fallback path.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Potential NPE when all-clients resource type is not yet created

In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when the per-client resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` which can return null (e.g., if resource type resource was never created, or `supportsAuthorizationSchema` returns false). The result is then passed directly into `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` without a null check, risking an NPE instead of gracefully returning false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
hasPermission(String) looks up resource with swapped name/id arguments, likely always failing

In `hasPermission(String scope)`, `resourceStore.findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, server.getId())` passes the resource server's id as the owner argument. Compare with `getOrCreateResource`/`hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` which use `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` differently, and with `AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource` which does a plain `findByName(resourceServer, type.getType())` without an owner. If the `findByName(ResourceServer, String name, String owner)` overload actually requires the resource owner (not server id) to match the stored resource's owner, this lookup can fail to find the all-clients resource (created with `resourceServer.getClientId()` as owner in `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`), causing `canManageClientScopes()`/`canView(ClientScopeModel)` to always return false even when an all-clients permission exists. This diverges from the correct pattern used elsewhere (`AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource`), and should use the same consistent lookup rather than owner=server.getId().

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3, breaking existing contract

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was previously 4 and is now changed to 3, while FEATURE_DISABLED takes the old value 4. Any existing scripts or documentation relying on exit code 4 meaning 'recreate upgrade needed' will now get incorrect behavior (3 now means recreate, 4 means feature disabled). This is a breaking change to a documented exit-code contract for a preview feature; it should be called out explicitly as a behavior change, and existing automation relying on these codes could silently misinterpret results.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds resource IDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, resourceStore.findByType is used to iterate resources of type GROUPS, and granted.add(groupResource.getId()) adds the *resource* ID, not the group's model ID. Unlike GroupPermissions (V1) which strips the RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX off the resource name to recover the group ID, V2 resources are created with resource name == group ID (per AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup), so resource.getId() is the authorization resource's internal ID, not the group ID. This will return a set of resource IDs that callers (e.g. UsersResource, session.users().getUsersCount(realm, groupIds)) expect to be actual group IDs, causing user/group filtering based on group membership to silently fail (return no users or wrong set).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
Group resource name uses group ID, not stable identifier semantics inconsistent with user resource naming

resolveGroup returns group.getId() similarly to resolveUser returning user.getId(), but getResourceName() special-cases USERS to map resource.getName() to username while GROUPS has no equivalent branch, so getResourceName for group resources will just return resource.getDisplayName() (likely the raw group id) instead of a human-readable group name. This leaves the UI/representation showing the group id rather than the group name, inconsistent with the Users resource type behavior added in the same change.

canList() role check narrowed, removing VIEW_USERS/MANAGE_USERS short-circuit note

canList() was changed to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()`. canView() internally checks MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles so behavior is preserved, but the diff removed explicit AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS/MANAGE_USERS from the role check in canList and now solely relies on canView() which, in GroupPermissionsV2, performs an authorization policy evaluation hitting the store (hasPermission) even for simple admin-role checks. This introduces extra avoidable policy evaluation overhead on every list check versus the previous hasOneAdminRole short-circuit covering more roles directly.

grantIfNoPermission logic changed without accounting for group-based filtering correctly

toRepresentation() calls usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null) to decide whether canView() should default-grant when there's no explicit permission setup. Previously the group attribute was only set when `!auth.users().canView()`; now it's set whenever groupIds is non-empty regardless of whether the user already has full view permission. This changes grantIfNoPermission's effective semantics subtly (session attribute set even when user canView() is true), which could cause unintended default-grant behavior in edge cases depending on how canView()/grantIfNoPermission interact across requests using the same session.

The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
English reference file path derivation is fragile and may fail silently

englishFile is computed via two regex replaceAll calls on the absolute path ("resources-community"→"resources" and locale suffix→"_en.properties"). This assumes a specific directory naming convention and will break (or silently point to a nonexistent/incorrect file) for any theme file whose path doesn't match these exact substrings, e.g. files already under "resources" (not "resources-community") where the first replaceAll is a no-op but still works, but any renamed/variant theme directories or files with unexpected naming (e.g. containing "resources-community" as part of another word) would silently produce a wrong path. There's no validation that englishFile exists; the FileInputStream will throw a plain IOException wrapped in RuntimeException, which is harder to diagnose than a clear error referencing the actual theme/key being checked.

containsHtml regex may false-negative for self-closing or uppercase tags HTML_TAGS pattern `<[a-z]+[^>]*>` only matches lowercase tag names and does not account for self-closing tags like `
` without a space, or tags with uppercase letters. If the English source uses a tag not matching this pattern (e.g., `
` or malformed markup), containsHtml returns false, causing the stricter POLICY_NO_HTML to be applied even though English technically contains HTML-like markup, potentially producing false-positive 'Illegal HTML' errors in translations that mirror the English content.

santizeAnchors mutates value incrementally during find() iteration, risking IndexOutOfBounds/incorrect removal with duplicate anchors

The loop calls `matcher.find()` on the original `value` string, but `value` itself is updated inside the loop body via replaceFirst. Because `matcher` keeps iterating over the original string snapshot (Matcher is bound to the original CharSequence, not the mutated `value` variable), find() positions and group() text no longer correspond to the current state of `value` once replacements have happened, especially when the same anchor tag occurs multiple times. This can produce incorrect sanitization results for messages with repeated or multiple anchor tags, though it won't throw since Matcher operates on the original immutable string, but results are quietly wrong for multi-anchor messages.

verifySafeHtml wraps IOExceptions from reading `file` and `englishFile` in unchecked RuntimeException and lets them propagate out of verify(), while verify() itself only declares/catches MojoExecutionException for the Files.readString call. This means the exception types mismatch: verifyNoDuplicateKeys errors are handled via MojoExecutionException while verifySafeHtml errors escape as RuntimeException, producing inconsistent error handling/reporting behavior for the Maven plugin (likely results in a raw stack trace rather than a clean message during the build).

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

Backward-compat token ids without ':' prefix accepted silently

Unchecked raw List type used for recovery code comparisons

Any aliased form like `count() as total`, `count(id)`, or columns with extra whitespace inside parentheses won't be transformed, silently leaving regular (non-upsampled) counts for queries that should be upsampled. This is a brittle approach compared to parsing the actual function AST already used elsewhere in the codebase (event_search parsing).

Error-focused detection relies only on raw query string containment

_is_error_focused_query does a naive substring check for "event.type:error" in the lowercased query string. This will produce false positives/negatives for queries like `!event.type:error` (negation) or `message:"event.type:error"` as literal text, or when combined with OR logic in different environments. This can cause upsampling to be wrongly applied/not applied for the discover dataset, directly affecting event counts shown to users.

The comment states "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution," but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called separately in `_get_event_stats` for every closure invocation (top events, rpc, standard), including repeated calls in `get_event_stats_factory` for split-decision requests (errors_only_query, transactions_only_query, original query) which use different `query` strings each time. Since `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` depends on `request.GET` query content, not the varied `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`, this can lead to inconsistent upsampling decisions between the split sub-queries (e.g. error-only vs full query) even though the comment implies a single consistent decision was cached for the whole request.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` catches bare `Exception` twice and silently ignores failures, including type errors from malformed `contexts` structures. This can mask bugs in test setup where sample_rate is silently not set, making test failures confusing to debug, and is overly broad for test utility code that should fail loudly on unexpected input.

Test for upsampled count asserts implausible fixed values without verifying actual sample_weight derivation

`test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` based on a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, assuming sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10. This test doesn't verify that `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` is actually computed and stored correctly end-to-end (depends on `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in factories.py and the `sample_weight` column population), so if that chain breaks the test might still pass with coincidental values 1 or fail with an unrelated error, not clearly diagnosing the upsampling math itself.

If index building for many namespaces takes a long time (which is exactly the motivation for this PR), the server constructor itself can hang indefinitely or for a very long time, blocking the whole application startup (and anything depending on ResourceServer creation, e.g. module server wiring). This moves the problem from a gRPC call's context cancellation to blocking overall process startup, which can be worse for large/slow deployments and provides no way to bound or observe the delay before serving traffic.

Init is no longer idempotently callable per-request, removing safety net for lazy failures

Previously every RPC method called s.Init(ctx) defensively, ensuring the server was initialized before serving (and returning init errors to callers). That per-call guard was removed from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. If NewResourceServer's Init succeeds partially (sync.Once only runs once) or if some external code path manages to construct a `server` struct without going through NewResourceServer, the server will serve requests referencing unitialized state (e.g. broadcaster not set) causing nil pointer dereferences (e.g. in Watch calling s.broadcaster.Subscribe) rather than a clean error.

Non-atomic totalBatchesIndexed increment under concurrent goroutines

In searchSupport.init, totalBatchesIndexed++ is executed inside group.Go goroutines that run concurrently (group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) allows multiple workers), but totalBatchesIndexed is a plain int incremented without synchronization. This is a data race and can produce incorrect/undercounted totals in the emitted span event, and under -race will be flagged as a race condition.

ListIterator still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracePrefix+"List")` and discards the derived ctx, so trace context is not propagated into listAtRevision/listLatest and their nested spans, unlike the fix applied to GetResourceStats in the same PR. This leaves traces still disconnected for the List path, which the PR claims to fix generally.

false_positives.candidate:
queue.Queue.shutdown() does not exist before Python 3.13

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both `Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13 (PEP 578 / bpo-... added in 3.13). Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12 in production, so this call will raise `AttributeError`/`AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'` at runtime. Because the call is wrapped in a bare `except Exception: logger.exception(...)`, the error is swallowed, but the net effect is that worker threads are never actually signaled to stop (they remain blocked in `work_queue.get()`), causing `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` to time out on every shutdown and the daemon threads to leak for the life of the process.

Workers can block forever on shutdown since queue has no sentinel/unblock mechanism

Since `queue.Queue.shutdown()` isn't available on the Python version in use (see above), there is no fallback mechanism (e.g. a sentinel value or `put_nowait`) to unblock worker threads doing a blocking `get()` on an empty queue. As a result, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` cannot reliably stop workers that are idle-waiting, leading to resource leaks (threads never terminate) and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` effectively not fully cleaning up, which could keep stale state (open sentry_sdk transactions, DB connections, etc.) running after the strategy is supposedly closed.

get_committable_offsets does an O(gap) linear scan every second

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every tick of the 1-second commit loop. If a message is delayed/stuck (e.g. a slow group) while many offsets pile up behind it, this becomes a large linear scan repeated every second, consuming CPU proportional to the gap size. Given the stated motivation of the PR is to avoid slow items blocking the pipeline, a slow item can still cause this scan to balloon, partially offsetting the perf benefit this PR intends to deliver.

WorkItem retains full Message object unnecessarily, inflating queue memory

`WorkItem` stores the entire original `message` (including the raw Kafka payload) even though only `partition`, `offset`, and the decoded `result` are ever used by `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. For a backlog of thousands of queued items (which this feature expects to build up when a group is slow), this needless retention of the raw message/payload bytes in every work item increases memory pressure substantially.

max_workers=0 silently falls back to default num_queues

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` treats `max_workers=0` the same as `None`, falling back to the default of 20 queues instead of raising an error or honoring an explicit (if nonsensical) value of 0. This could mask a configuration mistake silently.

Queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash() for consistent routing

`get_queue_for_group` uses the builtin `hash(group_key)` to pick a queue index. Python's string hashing is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) by default, so while this is consistent for the lifetime of a single process (satisfying in-process ordering guarantees), it is non-deterministic across process restarts/rebalances. This isn't a functional bug given the stated invariants, but is worth calling out as fragile/surprising if used anywhere assuming cross-process determinism (e.g. tests asserting fixed indices, or future features relying on sticky partitioning across restarts).

`use_optimized` is derived from a plain client-supplied query parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) with no CSRF/signing protection, and `enable_advanced` relies on `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`. Combined with `OptimizedCursorPaginator`'s negative-offset feature (see paginator.py), this lets any user who happens to have global org access (not necessarily a true superuser) opt into bypassing normal offset bounds. There's no rate limiting or validation that negative offsets stay within sane bounds, so this could be used to scan/exfiltrate audit log entries outside the intended paginated window or cause excessive DB load. At minimum this is an unvetted, security-sensitive code path that should not be toggled by a public query string.

The redirect-chasing loop bound was reduced from 10000 to 1000 without adjusting (or re-validating) the previously documented caveat: 'this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the bound to 1000 makes incorrect joins now possible for segment trees of depth >1000 instead of >10000, a significant regression in correctness for deep span trees, and the explanatory comment was deleted so future maintainers won't know why/how this limit interacts with correctness.

The script switched from `sadd`/`sunionstore` (plain set semantics, union does not merge/overwrite values) to `zunionstore` using span payloads as members and timestamps as scores. `zunionstore` aggregates scores by default via SUM when the same member exists in both sets, which is likely never intended here (payloads should be unique per span so this may not trigger immediately, but is semantically fragile). More importantly, this change introduces eviction logic in lines 62-64 (`zpopmin` when span_count > 1000) that silently discards the lowest-scored (oldest timestamp) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. This is a data-loss change: spans that overflow the limit are silently dropped from the segment rather than being flagged/logged, which will corrupt or truncate large segments without any observability (contrast with the Python-side `_load_segment_data`, which explicitly logs and metrics when max_segment_bytes is exceeded, but the max_segment_spans python-side guard was removed in this PR, see buffer.py diff removing the span-count-exceeded check).

The diff removes the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and logged/metriced 'segment_span_count_exceeded', deleting the segment from processing with visibility. This safety net is now solely delegated to the new Lua-side zpopmin eviction (add-buffer.lua), which silently drops data with no logging/metrics at all. This is a loss of observability for an already risky operation (truncating a segment), and the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now effectively dead/unused in this file (still accepted as a constructor arg but never enforced), which is misleading to future readers of the code.

No test coverage added for new 1000-span eviction behavior

The PR title and lua changes introduce span eviction when count exceeds 1000, but no test in test_buffer.py exercises this path (e.g., processing >1000 spans in a segment and asserting that only the most recent 1000 are kept, or that evicted spans are dropped as expected). Given this is a data-dropping behavior change, it should have explicit test coverage verifying the eviction count and which spans are retained/dropped.

Cross-org cache key collision risk from using hash()

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for ints is stable per-process but PYTHONHASHSEED randomization affects strings/some types; more importantly hash() is not guaranteed collision-free, and across different processes/workers hashing may differ (not an issue here since ints hash to themselves), but combining org id with a non-cryptographic hash of a short list has real collision risk is low but using str(project_ids) would be simpler and safer. More critically, the cache value is a simple boolean with no versioning: if `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes, cached entries for up to 60s will serve stale eligibility, silently flipping which aggregation (count vs sum(sample_weight)) is applied — causing incorrect counts returned to users with no error during the window.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact string `count()` (after lowering/stripping). Any aliased form like `count() as total`, `count(id)`, or columns with extra whitespace inside parentheses won't be transformed, silently leaving regular (non-upsampled) counts for queries that should be upsampled. This is a brittle approach compared to parsing the actual function AST already used elsewhere in the codebase (event_search parsing).

Error-focused detection relies only on raw query string containment

_is_error_focused_query does a naive substring check for "event.type:error" in the lowercased query string. This will produce false positives/negatives for queries like `!event.type:error` (negation) or `message:"event.type:error"` as literal text, or when combined with OR logic in different environments. This can cause upsampling to be wrongly applied/not applied for the discover dataset, directly affecting event counts shown to users.

The comment states "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution," but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called separately in `_get_event_stats` for every closure invocation (top events, rpc, standard), including repeated calls in `get_event_stats_factory` for split-decision requests (errors_only_query, transactions_only_query, original query) which use different `query` strings each time. Since `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` depends on `request.GET` query content, not the varied `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`, this can lead to inconsistent upsampling decisions between the split sub-queries (e.g. error-only vs full query) even though the comment implies a single consistent decision was cached for the whole request.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` catches bare `Exception` twice and silently ignores failures, including type errors from malformed `contexts` structures. This can mask bugs in test setup where sample_rate is silently not set, making test failures confusing to debug, and is overly broad for test utility code that should fail loudly on unexpected input.

Test for upsampled count asserts implausible fixed values without verifying actual sample_weight derivation

`test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` based on a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, assuming sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10. This test doesn't verify that `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` is actually computed and stored correctly end-to-end (depends on `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in factories.py and the `sample_weight` column population), so if that chain breaks the test might still pass with coincidental values 1 or fail with an unrelated error, not clearly diagnosing the upsampling math itself.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The new permDenialCache stores a 'denied' result for `shortCacheTTL` (30s) keyed by namespace/user/action/name/parent. If a user is denied access and then permissions change (e.g. they are granted access, or create the resource) within that 30s window, the Check() call will short-circuit to a cached denial at line 117-121 without re-querying the DB, returning Allowed=false even though the user now has access. This directly undermines the stated goal of the PR (allowing users to access resources they just created), since any earlier failed check for the same name/action will keep denying access for up to 30 seconds afterward.

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns permissions but checkPermission(ctx, cachedPerms, checkReq) returns false (stale/incomplete cache), the code falls through to call getIdentityPermissions, which for TypeUser/TypeServiceAccount calls GetUserIdentifiers (and getUserBasicRole/getUserTeams) again. ProvideAuthZClient now passes `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` for the in-proc client instead of a real cache (previously a `cache.NewLocalCache` was used). If the server-side cache has a cache miss or needs singleflight dedup under load, this adds overhead for every single authorization check in-proc that was previously avoided by the client cache; the PR description claims this is intentional for resolving stale-cache resource-creation issues, but it removes a layer of caching for all other read-heavy authz checks that aren't related to freshly-created resources.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
process.kill() now gated behind a broken isinstance check, preventing restart of hung/crashed processes

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the call to `process.kill()` is now wrapped in `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):`. However, processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process` with a 'spawn' context (`multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process`), which returns a `SpawnProcess` instance. `SpawnProcess` does NOT subclass `multiprocessing.Process` (the default context's Process class) — both only share a common base `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`. Therefore `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for the actual spawned worker processes, and `kill()` is silently skipped. Previously (pre-PR) `process.kill()` was called unconditionally (wrapped only in try/except ValueError), so it worked correctly. With this change, hung or crashed flusher processes are never actually killed before a replacement process is spawned to handle the same shards, leading to zombie/leaked processes that may still be alive and could continue producing to Kafka or interacting with Redis concurrently with the new process for the same shards — risking duplicate segment production and resource leaks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: flusher processes created via spawn context are SpawnProcess instances, which are not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance guard is always false and process.kill() is never called for hung processes.

false_positives.candidate:
queue.Queue.shutdown() does not exist before Python 3.13

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown`. Both `Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13 (PEP 578 / bpo-... added in 3.13). Sentry currently targets Python 3.11/3.12 in production, so this call will raise `AttributeError`/`AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'` at runtime. Because the call is wrapped in a bare `except Exception: logger.exception(...)`, the error is swallowed, but the net effect is that worker threads are never actually signaled to stop (they remain blocked in `work_queue.get()`), causing `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` to time out on every shutdown and the daemon threads to leak for the life of the process.

Workers can block forever on shutdown since queue has no sentinel/unblock mechanism

Since `queue.Queue.shutdown()` isn't available on the Python version in use (see above), there is no fallback mechanism (e.g. a sentinel value or `put_nowait`) to unblock worker threads doing a blocking `get()` on an empty queue. As a result, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` cannot reliably stop workers that are idle-waiting, leading to resource leaks (threads never terminate) and `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` effectively not fully cleaning up, which could keep stale state (open sentry_sdk transactions, DB connections, etc.) running after the strategy is supposedly closed.

get_committable_offsets does an O(gap) linear scan every second

`get_committable_offsets` iterates `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every tick of the 1-second commit loop. If a message is delayed/stuck (e.g. a slow group) while many offsets pile up behind it, this becomes a large linear scan repeated every second, consuming CPU proportional to the gap size. Given the stated motivation of the PR is to avoid slow items blocking the pipeline, a slow item can still cause this scan to balloon, partially offsetting the perf benefit this PR intends to deliver.

WorkItem retains full Message object unnecessarily, inflating queue memory

`WorkItem` stores the entire original `message` (including the raw Kafka payload) even though only `partition`, `offset`, and the decoded `result` are ever used by `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. For a backlog of thousands of queued items (which this feature expects to build up when a group is slow), this needless retention of the raw message/payload bytes in every work item increases memory pressure substantially.

max_workers=0 silently falls back to default num_queues

`num_queues=max_workers or 20` treats `max_workers=0` the same as `None`, falling back to the default of 20 queues instead of raising an error or honoring an explicit (if nonsensical) value of 0. This could mask a configuration mistake silently.

Queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash() for consistent routing

`get_queue_for_group` uses the builtin `hash(group_key)` to pick a queue index. Python's string hashing is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED) by default, so while this is consistent for the lifetime of a single process (satisfying in-process ordering guarantees), it is non-deterministic across process restarts/rebalances. This isn't a functional bug given the stated invariants, but is worth calling out as fragile/surprising if used anywhere assuming cross-process determinism (e.g. tests asserting fixed indices, or future features relying on sticky partitioning across restarts).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cross-org cache key collision risk from using hash()

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for ints is stable per-process but PYTHONHASHSEED randomization affects strings/some types; more importantly hash() is not guaranteed collision-free, and across different processes/workers hashing may differ (not an issue here since ints hash to themselves), but combining org id with a non-cryptographic hash of a short list has real collision risk is low but using str(project_ids) would be simpler and safer. More critically, the cache value is a simple boolean with no versioning: if `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes, cached entries for up to 60s will serve stale eligibility, silently flipping which aggregation (count vs sum(sample_weight)) is applied — causing incorrect counts returned to users with no error during the window.

Error-focused detection relies only on raw query string containment

The comment states "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution," but `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called separately in `_get_event_stats` for every closure invocation (top events, rpc, standard), including repeated calls in `get_event_stats_factory` for split-decision requests (errors_only_query, transactions_only_query, original query) which use different `query` strings each time. This can mask bugs in test setup where sample_rate is silently not set, making test failures confusing to debug, and is overly broad for test utility code that should fail loudly on unexpected input.

`test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` based on a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`, assuming sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10. When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns permissions but checkPermission(ctx, cachedPerms, checkReq) returns false (stale/incomplete cache), the code falls through to call getIdentityPermissions, which for TypeUser/TypeServiceAccount calls GetUserIdentifiers (and getUserBasicRole/getUserTeams) again. getCachedIdentityPermissions always returns cache.ErrNotFound for types.TypeRenderService (line 353-355), forcing getIdentityPermissions -> getRendererPermissions to be computed on every single Check/List call for renderer identities, even though the result is static and cheap to cache. ProvideAuthZClient now passes `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` for the in-proc client instead of a real cache (previously a `cache.NewLocalCache` was used). If the server-side cache has a cache miss or needs singleflight dedup under load, this adds overhead for every single authorization check in-proc that was previously avoided by the client cache; the PR description claims this is intentional for resolving stale-cache resource-creation issues, but it removes a layer of caching for all other read-heavy authz checks that aren't related to freshly-created resources.

In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the async legacy write goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the original request ctx as parent. If the HTTP request context is cancelled/finishes (as it normally does once the response is returned to the client), the derived context is cancelled immediately, so the legacy write will likely fail with context canceled before the 10s timeout has a chance to elapse. This defeats the purpose of the async legacy write (reliability net) in mode 3, silently causing legacy writes to fail most of the time in production. The context passed to the goroutine should be detached from the parent request context (e.g., using `context.WithoutCancel` or a fresh context with request-scoped values copied) before adding the timeout.

No rollback/compensation when legacy write fails in mode 3 async path

Because the legacy write happens asynchronously after the unified storage write succeeds, there's no mechanism (retry, dead-letter, reconciliation) to catch or compensate when the legacy write fails (errObjectSt != nil only gets fed into a metric, nothing else). Given this is explicitly described as a 'safe measure' for keeping legacy in sync, silently dropping failures could lead to drift between legacy and unified storage with no operator-visible signal besides a metric. The PR doesn't address detection/alerting/retry for this gap.

No tests verify async legacy write behavior of mode 3

All tests for mode3 only verify that the Storage (unified) call result is used/returned; none of the tests assert that the Legacy mock's Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection methods are actually invoked (asynchronously) with correct arguments, nor do they test the new timeout/cancellation behavior. Given mode3's entire purpose is to also write to legacy storage, this is a significant test gap — a regression that stops the async legacy write entirely would not be caught by this suite.

set_locale now calls I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! on every controller request, which iterates up to 3 locales (user, site default, en) and calls I18n.ensure_loaded! for each, acquiring LOAD_MUTEX each time. Although load_locale returns early if already loaded, this still means every request now runs the mutex-synchronized membership check 2-3x instead of once, adding unnecessary contention/overhead especially under multi-threaded Puma/Unicorn with many concurrent requests.

translate still only loads config.locale, not fallback locales

The patched translate method only ensures config.locale is loaded (load_locale(config.locale)), but with fallbacks now enabled via I18n::Backend::Fallbacks, a translation lookup for the current locale may need to fall through to SiteSetting.default_locale or :en translations which are never explicitly loaded by this accelerator. Since Base#load_translations is overridden to require explicit loading of files, translations for fallback locales other than config.locale may never actually be loaded into the backend unless something else triggers it (e.g. the controller's set_locale calling ensure_loaded! for all fallbacks). This creates a fragile coupling: translate() depends on an external before_filter to pre-load fallback locales, so any I18n.t call made before set_locale runs (e.g. during console/rake tasks, background jobs, or early boot) can silently return missing-translation results instead of falling back correctly.

FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale at lookup time, which is fine lazily, but note this initializer unconditionally overwrites I18n.fallbacks for all environments (removed previously environment-specific config.i18n.fallbacks = true toggles). There's no longer any way to disable fallbacks per-environment as previously supported in production/profile configs, which were removed. If fallbacks are undesired in some environment (e.g. test, to catch missing translation keys precisely), this is now a global behavior change with no opt-out, differing from previous per-environment configurability.

TopicEmbed.import mutates its `contents` argument in place via `contents << ...` to append the import footer (topic_embed.rb line 13), and poll_feed passes `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` built fresh each iteration, so this isn't a major issue here, but combined with `absolutize_urls`, raw remote HTML content from an RSS feed is directly rendered with cook_method raw_html and never sanitized (no `sanitize` gem usage), meaning any HTML/JS in the feed content is stored and rendered as-is in the post. true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same TopicEmbed.import concerns: unsafe in-place appending to contents and XSS from unsanitized imported HTML. Although it does not explicitly mention the nil NoMethodError or URL interpolation, it identifies the same underlying code risks.

The migration sets `updatedAt` with `DEFAULT NOW()` but the Prisma schema marks the field `@default(now()) @updatedAt`. Prisma's @updatedAt expects the column to auto-update on every write via Prisma Client, but any direct SQL writes/upserts bypassing Prisma (e.g. raw queries) will not update this field automatically, and existing rows retroactively get 'NOW()' as updatedAt at migration time which is misleading since it doesn't reflect actual last-cache-update time, undermining the newly added cache-status UI feature.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds called on every connectedCalendars query without caching

`connectedCalendars.handler.ts` calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` on every request to `connectedCalendars`, adding an additional groupBy query per request. For users/orgs with many credentials this could add noticeable DB load; there's no memoization or batching optimization, and this new query runs regardless of whether the UI actually needs cache status (e.g., non-Google calendar integrations).

cacheUpdatedAt uses || null, converting falsy-but-valid timestamps incorrectly

`cacheStatusMap.get(calendar.credentialId) || null` will treat a valid Date object as falsy only if it's literally falsy, which Date objects never are, so this isn't actually buggy for Date values — but it silently swallows the distinction between 'no cache status found' and 'found but value is null', which could mask bugs if getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ever returns `{credentialId, updatedAt: undefined}`. Low risk but worth tightening to explicit undefined check for clarity and correctness guarantees.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Reminders are only deleted on next cron run after reaching retryCount 2, allowing one extra retry/duplication window

After a reminder fails twice, retryCount becomes 2, but the current run's deleteMany query runs before the update loop and only deletes rows with retryCount > 1 (i.e. existing reminders from a prior run). This means a reminder that just hit retryCount=2 in this run will still be re-processed in the next cron invocation before being deleted, since the delete step always runs first and would only catch it on the *following* run - meaning the reminder could be retried indefinitely if continually caught right at the boundary and twilio.scheduleSMS is retried for the same booking without respecting the already-incremented retry count the same cycle. If `message` or `sendTo` ends up falsy, the if-block at line 158 is skipped entirely with no retryCount increment and no logging, so these reminders remain in scheduled=false, retryCount=0 state forever, retried every cron run without ever being cleaned up or flagged as failing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys don't do what's intended

The schema uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` as object keys. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a dynamic/generic key matching any string field name; it produces a fixed literal string (e.g. "[object Object]"), so these computed properties define a single, meaningless property name rather than validating 'any additional numeric/unknown fields'. Combined with Zod's default behavior of stripping unrecognized keys from a parsed object, this means that when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is on, the parsed/stored token data will silently drop fields like `expiry_date`/`refresh_token` that aren't explicitly `access_token`, defeating the purpose of this schema and corrupting stored credentials for self-hosters using credential sync.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in minimumTokenResponseSchema: computed keys built from z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() are invalid/meaningless and do not validate arbitrary fields as intended. The candidate adds impact details but points to the same underlying code issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw unparsed fetch Response, inconsistent with refreshFunction's return shape

When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw `fetch()` Response object directly without calling `.json()`. However, callers assume the shape returned by `refreshFunction()`, which varies per app (e.g. Google Calendar's refreshFunction resolves to `fetchTokens.res`, an object with a `.data` property, not a Response). Code such as `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data;` will get `undefined` when the self-hosted sync endpoint is used, since a Response object has no `.data` field, breaking token refresh silently when CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is configured. Similarly in HubSpot's CalendarService the sync-path response is used directly as if it were the already-parsed HubspotToken object (accessing `.expiresIn`), which won't exist on an unparsed fetch Response.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same return-shape mismatch: the sync-enabled refresh path returns a raw fetch Response, while Google and HubSpot callers expect parsed token objects, causing incorrect handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing `prisma` import causes compile/runtime failure

A malformed or incorrectly-encrypted `keys` payload will throw an unhandled exception, resulting in an unstructured 500 error instead of a clear 400 'invalid payload' response, making debugging harder for self-hosters integrating with this endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

deleteScheduledEmailReminder/SMS calls not awaited

The forEach loop calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting the promises. Since the cancel API handler returns right after, and these calls perform async DB writes (setting `cancelled: true`), the response may complete before the cancellation flag is actually persisted, increasing the race window where the cron job's query (within the same cron tick) might miss marking it cancelled before the response is used by the client to assume cancellation succeeded fully. It also means errors are not propagated to the caller for retries/logging context tied to the specific booking cancellation flow.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are invoked without await inside forEach, so scheduled reminder cancellation may not complete reliably and errors are not propagated.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation and new scheduling race within same cron run

The cron job first cancels reminders flagged `cancelled: true` scheduled within the next hour, then later finds unscheduled reminders and schedules new emails. There's no check that excludes already-cancelled bookingUids/workflowStepIds from this unscheduled-reminders query, so if a reminder was cancelled (cancelled=true) but not yet caught by the 1-hour window pass, it could still be picked up and sent since the `unscheduledReminders` query filters only on `scheduled: false` without excluding `cancelled: true` reminders. This re-introduces a path for cancelled reminders to be sent.

Deleted reminders no longer deleted from DB in update handler

Previously, after cancelling scheduled reminders when event types are removed from a workflow, the code also deleted the WorkflowReminder DB rows (`deleteReminderPromise`/`ctx.prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany`). This deletion was removed; now only `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are called, which for EMAIL just sets `cancelled: true` (not deleted) unless `immediateDelete` is passed (it is not passed here). false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes stored in plaintext array without hashing/removal consistency

Backup codes are generated and encrypted as a blob, but each code remains a plaintext secret within that blob. When one code is used (next-auth-options.ts), it is replaced with null but the array length/order persists; there's no indication other than null to users which codes remain used. More importantly, codes are never hashed before storage—only the whole JSON array is symmetrically encrypted. If CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever compromised, all backup codes are exposed in plaintext, unlike typical implementations where backup codes are hashed individually (similar to passwords). This is a weaker security posture than TOTP secret handling for sensitive, one-time credentials.

`const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` infers backupCodes as never[], relying on implicit any assignment from setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes) where body is untyped JSON. There's no runtime validation that body.backupCodes is actually a string array, so a malformed/missing response could cause .map() to throw or silently render nothing without clear error handling.

Calling /setup regenerates backupCodes and persists them to the DB immediately (before the user confirms via /enable). If a user starts setup but never completes it (abandons at QR step), stale backup codes remain stored on the user record while twoFactorEnabled is false. These codes could later be reactivated by just calling /enable without ever being re-shown to the user, since enable.ts (not shown) presumably doesn't regenerate backup codes. This creates a risk of a backup code set associated with a now-stale/forgotten secret being usable without the owner's current knowledge of them, and multiple incomplete setup attempts quietly overwrite previous codes with no audit trail.

Backup code match doesn't invalidate/remove the used code

In disable.ts, after finding `index` for the supplied backup code, the comment says "we delete all stored backup codes at the end, no need to do this here" — this is true for disable flow since all backupCodes/twoFactorSecret are nulled below. However the index variable is computed but never used otherwise; this works accidentally only because disable always wipes everything. If this logic is ever reused elsewhere (e.g. refactored into a shared helper for other backup-code consuming endpoints), failing to invalidate the specific used code would allow reuse of the same backup code multiple times. There's no shared single-use enforcement abstraction, raising future reuse risk.

No E2E coverage for backup-code login or disable-via-backup-code flow

The PR description states backup codes can be used for login (clicking 'Lost access') and for disabling 2FA, but the only test changes added are around the backup-codes-download/copy/close UI during setup. The TODO comment explicitly acknowledges missing tests: 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. This leaves the core new login-with-backup-code and disable-with-backup-code logic (including single-use invalidation) completely untested, despite being significant new auth-critical code paths.

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) is wrapped in a try/catch, but forEach does not await the async callbacks. Previously (sync code) a thrown error inside the callback would propagate synchronously and be caught by the surrounding try/catch. Now that the callback is async and awaits getCalendar(), any error thrown inside becomes a rejected Promise that is never awaited, so it escapes the try/catch entirely and becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being logged via logger.error. The function also returns before all deletions settle, so callers relying on completion (e.g. before sending reschedule emails) might run concurrently with/ahead of the pending deletions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: async callbacks passed to forEach are not awaited, so errors become unhandled promise rejections that escape the surrounding try/catch, and the caller returns before the async deletions complete. The candidate's wording is more specific but describes the same fire-and-forget issue.

Making the callback async while using forEach means thrown/rejected errors from getCalendar()/deleteEvent() bypass the try/catch, resulting in silent/unhandled promise rejections rather than being logged.

forEach with async callback not awaited for calendar/video cleanup before sending reschedule emails

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... }) is fire-and-forget: the surrounding code (sendRequestRescheduleEmail, webhook dispatch) proceeds without waiting for these calendar/video deletions to finish or to catch their failures. Converting getCalendar to async made this race more pronounced, since previously the deletion happened synchronously or near-synchronously; now it's an unawaited microtask chain and any failures are swallowed as unhandled rejections.

Dynamic import() calls are still evaluated eagerly, not actually lazy

Each `import("./app")` call in the object literal executes immediately when this module is evaluated (as soon as `appStore` is imported anywhere), regardless of whether a given app is ever used. Simply storing the resulting Promise instead of awaiting it does not defer the module loading/bundling — bundlers like webpack will still create and request each chunk at the time this file runs. This negates the stated goal of the PR (async/lazy imports of app-store packages) while adding async/await overhead to every call site that previously did synchronous property access, with no actual reduction in initial load work for consumers who only need one app.

getCalendarCredentials still treats getCalendar as returning a value directly used downstream without documenting it's now a Promise

`const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` now stores a Promise<Calendar|null> in the `calendar` field of the returned structure (relying on later code awaiting `item.calendar`). This is a subtle API shape change (every consumer of getCalendarCredentials() must know to await `.calendar`) that is not documented via types/comments, making it easy for a future caller to accidentally treat it as a resolved Calendar object.

Nested async forEach for recurring-event calendar deletions remains unawaited

`bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })` pushes into apiDeletes asynchronously inside a forEach that isn't awaited by the enclosing code before `apiDeletes` is used in `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`.
